Indicators of economic activity and employment have continued to strengthen, but the overall tone is tempered by elevated and shock-driven inflation and a policy pivot toward tightening. The Committee’s 25 bp liftoff and guidance for ongoing increases plus balance-sheet reduction is consistent with Taylor-rule prescriptions when inflation significantly exceeds target and the labor market is tight, and with the literature on expectations management and balance-sheet policy (e.g., Svensson and Woodford on inflation-forecast targeting; Goodfriend on implementation tools). However, pandemic-induced supply-chain disruptions and COVID-related expenditure-weight distortions in measured CPI (as documented in work on pandemic inflation weighting) and the Russia–Ukraine energy-price shock imply a cost-push component that a flatter Phillips curve makes more costly to disinflate. Recent research on inflation-at-risk highlights fat right tails in the inflation distribution under such shocks, reinforcing the FOMC’s hawkish bias and aligning with Bullard’s dissent for a larger 50 bp move to re-anchor expectations. Emerging work on markups and profits during this period suggests part of the inflation impulse may be linked to rising markups, further complicating the growth–inflation trade-off. Net, while activity data are positive, the literature points to heightened inflation risks and policy-induced headwinds to growth, warranting a modestly positive but cautious sentiment.
